5a5c1bc8618665efea48444cc9083ae6590c2cf3.new: MAMBench establishes a verified, provenance-preserving data and agent foundation for studying memory-poisoning attacks against large language model (LLM) agents with external, persistent memory, and a benchmark, defence stack and evaluation built on it. This document reports the methodology of the project's seventeen phases: dataset identification and cleaning (Phase 1), a unified, validated benchmark substrate built on four conversational-memory datasets (Phase 2), a clean, memory-augmented question-answering agent evaluated against two third-party memory systems, Mem0 and A-MEM (Phase 3), a unified benchmark implementing seven structurally diverse memory-poisoning attacks against that unmodified agent (Phase 4), a general-purpose instrumentation, monitoring and attack-attribution layer built on the frozen Phase 3/4 evidence substrate (Phase 5), a governance defense evaluated against the same attack corpus and an external baseline (Phase 6), and the propagation, sleeper, forensic, risk-composition, learned-component, metric, utility, integrated and ablation-and-generalisation phases that follow (Phases 7-17). Phase 3's architecture was developed through five sequentially validated iterations and converged on a final composition, V3-Hybrid. A post-freeze revalidation pass found and fixed a reporting gap in the evaluation trace and scaled the campaign to a larger sample (n = 500/499/500 for Conditions A/B/C-Mem0, n = 120 for C-A-MEM): all three memory-equipped conditions correctly answer 76.4-84.2% of questions under LLM-judge scoring, against a 17.0% no-memory baseline — a large effect that a strict, conservative exact-match metric had understated by roughly a factor of 20 for gold-evidence generation. Phase 4 found that all seven attacks, under their own designed trigger conditions, wrote content into V3-Hybrid's memory and measurably influenced generated answers, confirmed by counterfactual masking. Phase 6's governance defense, evaluated in a four-signal factorial design (admission, retrieval, propagation and sleeper guards) against a 75-scenario poisoned-memory corpus, detects poisoning content at up to 100.0% at a 14.6% benign false-positive rate with the semantic consensus signal contributed back from Phase 11 (Section 26.10), and at 70.6% at a 7.3% false-positive rate without it, up from 47.1% at initial freeze after a validated false-positive fix, a threshold recalibrated against disjoint development data, the sleeper guard added to the full configuration and a regex coverage gap closed; it is compared against an unmodified external baseline (ASB's perplexity filter, which does not transfer to this threat model without recalibration and detects 0.0% at its own default threshold). Phase 7 resolves an open question from Phase 5's handoff report — whether FARMA's amplification cluster crowds out retrieval slots — with a repeatable measurement (re-entry rate 1.0 against a benign ceiling of 0.125), extends mechanism-level propagation studies to all seven attacks, and closes an embedding-based retrieval-pool-narrowing gap for two of them using a Mem0-backed two-stage pipeline (full closure for Sleeper Memory Poisoning, a partial result for AgentPoison). Phase 8 targets the sleeper/dormant-poisoning family with four detection signals over the retrieval pipeline. Its main finding is negative: the planted campaign artifact evades the content-structural signal entirely (it was never written as an imperative instruction), the one signal that catches it (activation shape) has a measured false-positive rate on ordinary benign memories (reduced from 47% to 17.6% by a refinement that preserves full sensitivity, but not eliminated), and no single signal is both sensitive to the attack and safe on benign content. Phase 9 reconstructs an attack's origin backward from a flagged incident (exposure, then full-chain lineage, then origin, then propagation), validated against all seven Phase 4 attacks: five reconstruct to a single, high-confidence origin, two (FARMA, MemoryGraft) correctly report multi-origin ambiguity rather than an arbitrary choice, and a benign incident correctly reports no attack origin. Phase 10 combines the signals of Phases 6-9 into one cross-guard risk estimate; an initial combined configuration regressed (47.1% versus 70.6% detection at the same false-positive rate), and a non-circular recalibration against disjoint development data — never the reported corpus — closed the gap, restoring detection to parity with the strongest prior configuration at no false-positive cost. Phase 11 investigates whether learned components (a relation-aware graph neural network and a gated linear network, both built from scratch) capture poisoning structure or semantics that the sanctioned rule-based signal vocabulary misses. Six negative or mixed findings (a data-scale detection ceiling, a benign-anomaly framing that collapsed to chance once a construction artifact was removed, a structural-feature confound from differences between collected and hand-authored corpora, clean- and poison-data expansion that left detection AUROC unchanged to three decimal places, and a semantic-relationship signal shown by a truthful-counterfactual control to be a text-format artifact) precede a fix: reusing the project's GROUPED_GATED rule composition as a second untrained reference score, combined by maximum rather than average or replacement, closes two leave-one-family-out generalization failures (0% to 100% and 50% to 100% detection) and raises an independent 7-attack corpus detector from 33.3% to 99.6% mean detection; the semantic signal this investigation surfaced was fed back into Phase 6, raising the reported B9/B10 configuration to 100.0% detection at 14.6% false-positive rate. Phase 12 defines four cross-cutting security metrics (Poison Admission Rate, Propagation Rate, Sleeper Detection Rate and Attribution/Mitigation Rate) plus a Defense Generalization Score over the B0–B8 evaluation matrix, ships a fifth defense component (a Consolidation Guard that re-checks a derivation's sources before persistence) after a position-robustness fix to the Propagation Rate measurement surfaced the gap, closes every borderline family miss (DSRM, FARMA, AgentPoison, MemoryGraft, MINJA) with root-caused fixes, and reports a cross-model-validated grand-mean Propagation Rate of 86.1% (2 local models × 3 distractor sets), with the new guard catching 100.0% of propagation events in every one of the 6 trials. Phase 13 runs the attribution layer described in Section 20 against corpus data at scale for the first time — all seven attribution types (origin, lineage, influence, exposure, references, propagation and the composed forensics/action layers), plus the Consolidation Guard's quarantine and allow decisions — achieving 100% source accuracy (15/15), 100% path fidelity including four constructed multi-source branches (19/19), and 100% influence and Consolidation Guard decision-tracing accuracy across every case tested. The correlation between admission-time and propagation-time confidence signals is weak and inconclusive at two independent resolutions, traced to near-binary signal firing on this corpus, and origin attribution's false-attribution rate under cross-attack ambiguity is untestable by construction, because testing it would require bypassing a ledger data-integrity invariant. Known limitations — the strictness of the multi-hop scoring ensemble (Section 32.34), a residual substring-matching gap in one additive metric, small absolute corpus sizes for the attack and defense evaluations, and an unresolved vendor identity-resolution question for A-MEM — are reported as explicit boundaries. Phases 14-17 are Sections 29-32, and Section 33 concludes across all of them.

__appendix__.heading: History of Corrections
paragraphs: This document states current results. Statements that later analyses superseded are listed here with the round in which they changed and the section that now holds the current result; the complete record of every review finding is docs/REMEDIATION_MASTER_REGISTER.md, and the Results Analysis lists the corrections to the results themselves.

Document form. Until 2026-10-19 this document was cumulative: each phase was written when completed, and later changes were added as dated, bracketed notes beside the original text. Those notes have been folded into the current text, and the superseded statements are summarised below.

Phase 6 detection (Sections 21.9, 25.5, 26.10). The B0-B8 corpus detection rose from 47.1% at initial freeze to 70.6% at 7.3% false positives (2026-09-17) and to 100.0% at 14.6% with the semantic consensus signal from Phase 11 (2026-09-20).

Phase 10 surfaces (Section 25.2). The risk-composition surfaces were first described as not wired into any live pipeline; Phase 14 wired the risk-band action into the live agent as B9, and round 7 evaluated the risk-weighted ranking and monitoring.

Related work (Section 2). A per-resource comparison of the registered benchmarks and defences was first left open; it was completed from primary sources on 2026-10-12 (docs/RELATED_WORK_AND_NOVELTY.md), which reclassified several contributions as adaptations of prior work.

Reproducibility (Sections 8 and 15). A dependency lock file and automatic code-state stamping were first listed as not provided, and a public release as undecided; the repository is public, requirements-ci.txt pins hashed versions for continuous integration, and the benchmark runner stamps every result with its git commit.

Mem0 live foundation (Section 32). A first Mem0 run reported 0/27 exclusions and attributed it to Mem0's smaller candidate pool; on 2026-09-28 this was traced to a scoring bug (a run-wide text lookup), and the corrected per-case result matches A-mem-sys (9/9).

Authorship confound (Section 32.12). The benign side of the generator/judge confound was first described as closed and attributed to content rather than authorship, and ConvoMem was cited as a human-written control; review round 3 (2026-09-28) withdrew both statements.

Harm study (Section 32.15). An early n=30 harm study reported harm dropping from 66.7% to 26.7% under B12 exclusion and was then read as harm dropping where B12 excludes often; the three-arm design and per-case reading showed neither holds.
Open items of rounds 1-2 (Section 32.10). The blinded human evaluation was listed as open; the project owner later rated all 60 items (Section 32.16).

Recommendation (Sections 32.42, 32.45, 32.56). Earlier rounds recommended B13 unqualified, then the union configurations, and in round 6 B18 (or B17) with evidence for memory poisoning and B14 or a deberta pass under a tight false-positive budget for injection-shaped text. Round 7 replaced these with the conditioned recommendation on clean hold-outs (Section 32.56).

Multi-hop performance (Section 32.34). Multi-hop reasoning was first declared outside what the benchmark measures, on the oracle condition's 36/60; the six-family re-run showed the ceiling to be the strictness of the scoring ensemble.

Exfiltration (Sections 32.40, 32.43). Four explanations were advanced for the family's zero harm before structural gates traced it to the generator omitting the recipient; the family was then tested on gate-valid instances.

Hold-out 3 (Sections 32.44, 32.49). Hold-out 3 was first counted as scored five times and its development set described as disjoint; round 7 counted seven scorings, found the development set overlapped the hold-out, relabelled the dependent comparisons as hold-out-calibrated, and retired the hold-out.

Rejection ledger (Sections 32.30, 32.31, 32.39). Adaptive evasion was recorded as open after the frozen-radius test and the first pre-registered re-test; the powered re-run in Section 32.39 resolved it.
Owner generalisation (Section 32.66). A 'threefold' owner-dependence of corroboration thresholds was reported on 2026-10-13 and withdrawn: it compared two benign budgets.
Working set (Section 32.57). A working-set figure of 123/157 that unioned in a leading probe was replaced by the committed 86/157 under the fixed probe rule.

Generalized union U-1 (abstract; Results Section 15). The union's benign false-positive rate on hold-out 8 was fixed by construction (register G3-4, remediation 2026-10-12); the shipped development-fitted anomaly signal needs per-owner benign calibration.

Operational closure (Sections 32.70-32.72, 33). The closure under the frozen rubric was 59%, 65% and 29% (provenance and governance, self-propagation, implicit sleepers) on 2026-10-14 and 64%, 65% and 34% after Defence v6 on 2026-10-15; the current scores after Defence v7 are 75.0%, 71.2% and 33.8%.

Three findings decompose it. First, attack validity: restricted to working attacks the gap narrows to 20.6 points (83.1% versus 62.5%) but remains significant at p=0.0001, so roughly 16 points are composition – the second hold-out is 21% working against the first's 31%. Second, the residual is not randomness. On the external corpora B14's decisions agree with the deberta classifier 90.1% of the time, with near-identical rates, and per item B14 catches what deberta scores near 1.0 and misses what it scores near 0; on this project's own attacks that agreement collapses and B14 is doing something else entirely. Third, B14 degrades across corpora worse than the component it tracks: deberta loses 18 points between the two hold-outs where B14 loses 37. Refitting B14 without deberta widens the gap (+32.9 to +46.6), so the deberta feature is load-bearing and the gap is a property of the fused weights (Section 32.47); the agreement evidence stands. The reason not to cite the higher figure alone is therefore mechanical rather than statistical.
